History:
• Presenting with wheeze and shortness of breath for 2–3 days.  
• Symptoms: exertional dyspnoea (unable to walk to work, occasional difficulty finishing sentences), dry cough, self-reported “fever” but measured 37 °C; no chest pain, no sputum, no haemoptysis, no nocturnal awakening; feels well at rest, can climb stairs.  
• Past episodes: childhood asthma “quite bad,” occasional hospital visits (not ICU); reports stopping regular inhalers 3–4 yrs ago yet later states salbutamol used every few weeks and before exercise (conflict noted).  
• Triggers/context: possible viral illness or seasonal pollen; no recent smoke/fume exposure.  
• Social: 33-y-o engineer, lives with partner, non-smoker, drinks ~1 glass wine every 2–3 days.  

Past Medical History:
• Asthma (childhood → intermittent adult symptoms).  
• Atopy: hay fever, eczema.  
• No other chronic illnesses reported.  
• Medications: Salbutamol inhaler PRN (dose/route/frequency not fully documented; uses “every few weeks” and before exercise). No hay-fever medication.  
• Allergies: Denies drug allergies.  
• Surgical / hospitalisations: asthma-related ED visits as a child; no ICU admissions.  

Physical Examination:
• Tele-consultation only; no direct exam.  
• Reported temperature 37 °C (afebrile).  
• No other vitals recorded.  
• Patient reports no chest pain, able to speak in full sentences at rest, ambulates indoors; no reported throat swelling or facial edema.  

Impression:
Likely acute asthma exacerbation, possibly triggered by viral infection or seasonal allergen exposure.  
DDx consistent with transcript:  
1. Acute asthma flare – fits history and symptoms.  
2. Viral upper-airway infection/acute bronchitis – dry cough, recent onset, could precipitate flare.  

Management Plan:
• Increase salbutamol: 2–4 puffs every 4 h via spacer.  
• Prescribe spacer device – pharmacist to demonstrate use.  
• Prescribe/issue peak-flow meter; record readings morning and evening for 1 week.  
• Start regular OTC oral antihistamine for hay fever (pharmacist to advise specific agent/dose).  
• Safety‐net: call clinic immediately if temperature rises, wheeze or breathlessness worsens, or peak-flow drops markedly.  
• Arrange asthma review in ~1 week (sooner if symptoms deteriorate) to assess control and consider additional controller therapy.  

Patient Summary:
33-year-old atopic patient with history of childhood asthma presents with 2–3 days of wheeze and exertional dyspnoea. Clinical picture suggests an acute asthma exacerbation likely precipitated by viral illness or allergens. Provided reliever-dose escalation, spacer, peak-flow monitoring, antihistamine, and follow-up plan.  

Key Takeaways:
• Use salbutamol 2–4 puffs every 4 h through the spacer until symptoms settle.  
• Monitor peak flow twice daily and seek help if readings fall or breathing worsens.  
• Begin daily antihistamine to reduce allergic triggers.  

Next Steps:
• Collect spacer and peak-flow meter from pharmacy; receive demonstration.  
• Record peak-flow values AM/PM for 7 days and report at follow-up.  
• Scheduled tele-review in 1 week (earlier if symptoms escalate).  

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing elements: heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, weight/BMI, full medication reconciliation.  
• Conflicts: patient says asthma meds stopped 3–4 yrs ago yet also reports ongoing salbutamol use (conflict noted).  
• Transcript quality: clear overall; occasional repetitions but clinically intelligible.
